summary: Partly. Analyzed HIR text is already meant to be a backend input, and for programs without modules it works today. It cannot carry real programs yet. hir/read.tcl rebuilds a full HIR from hir::format text, re-registers the type, struct, enum, trait and error declarations, and trusts the printed facts. Backend-facing facts are printed on purpose with read-back fallbacks: affine releases and moves, context installs and requirements, trait and context-trait clones, coroutine effects, `known` decisions and typed parameters. main.tcl already runs .hir files on every backend. On 7 module-free programs, the read-back HIR gave identical Core IR, identical specialized and generic NIR (one exception), and the same value on interp, compile, compile-hir, cranelift-generic and cranelift. Formatting cost about 2–5% of front-end time and reading about 15–25%. Four things stop it from being the boundary today. (1) Module sections are not serialized: there is no section scope, `modules` or `moduleScopeIds`, so any program that imports a source module does not read back. All 88 golden suites import `test`; traits-path fails at line 20, and several existing tests say this limit outright. (2) A String literal containing a newline is printed raw and breaks the line-based reader. (3) `boundsVerdicts` is not printed, so proven bounds checks stop being elided. This only affects speed: in 4 golden suites it was the only fact whose loss changed NIR, while losing the `semantic` instances, inferred/checked parameter contracts, calleeErrors, effectiveErrors and so on changed nothing. (4) Source spans and the `files` table are dropped: origins become synthetic `ir PATH`, and `-origins 1` text of a source HIR does not read back, so native error and allocation-site locations lose file:line. Separately, the in-memory HIR is not self-contained: native lowering reads process-global registries (struct registry and others), so a HIR fails native lowering after another program has been compiled in the same process. Reading text actually helps here, because it re-registers declarations. The boundary should be fully resolved and analyzed HIR. Static `compile:` decisions and trait monomorphization rebuild from syntax nodes, not from resolved HIR, so there is no clean 'resolved but unanalyzed' cut. Any earlier cut leaves analysis, decisions and monomorphization in Tcl, about 67–73% of front-end time on four golden suites. The Botlish front end would then replace little more than parsing and lowering (about 13–17%). Core IR is fully textual but is not a substitute: the native backend refuses it by design, and the Core IR `compile` path re-analyzes it with hir::build. Tcl can stay the orchestrator: a Botlish front end emits analyzed HIR text and Tcl reads it once per program, after the format gains module sections, newline-safe literals, bounds verdicts and (optionally) source spans.

summary: Compile-once already works inside one process, but only by convention. tests/golden/run.tcl compiles each suite once and runs that one HIR on four backends. No backend mutates the HIR (Tcl passes values, not references), and the NIR and Core IR come out byte-identical when regenerated with other backends run in between. The HIR value is not self-contained, though. hir::BuildOnce writes the program's declarations into about 11 process-wide registries: structs, enums, error payloads, traits, imports, and core::type/core::native for source-defined types. hir::lower, both Tcl compiler paths and native lowering read those registries rather than the HIR's own sourceTypes/errorDecls fields. So compiling a second program in between breaks the first one's run, or silently changes its results: interp and compile used the second program's `Small` domain. The golden 'compile' backend also calls back into the front end: it rebuilds HIR from Core IR with hir::build, re-running resolution, hygiene and every hir::check pass. That costs 0.7-1.6 s, 31-61% of the suite's own front-end time; core::compiler::evalHir (main.tcl's compile path) skips it. The native backends never call surface::*, BuildFull, the static decisions or warnings. Each run does its own native-only analyses (specialization with per-instance type inference, ranges, escape, ...), costing 3-7x the NIR emission and 10-30x the Rust driver; native::executable runs the specialization twice. The interp backend's preparation (hir::lower) is dominated by a quadratic helper. For caching across processes: storing the HIR dict string plus a snapshot of the registries let all five backends pass in a fresh process (loading takes milliseconds versus about 1.7 s of front end). The HIR alone fails on 4 of 5 backends, and the hir::format text does not round-trip a program with modules. For a Botlish front end with Tcl orchestration, that serialized HIR plus registries is a workable seam. But hir/ is not front-end-only code: the native backend calls about 20 hir namespaces, including type inference itself (hir::types::inferRegion), so that code stays in Tcl or gets duplicated. Front-end time: on small suites type inference is the biggest phase (14-18%), then parse (8-19%, mostly the first parse of library modules, cached per process), errorsets, hygiene, semantic instances, affine checks and mutvec elaboration. Parsing plus surface lowering is the cleanest part to split off but is cheap. On large suites the static-compile rounds repeat whole-program builds; an earlier measurement I did not reproduce gives signatures/type inference 39%, static-deps 14.5%, semantic instances 14.5%, hygiene 9%, parse 1.2%.

The backends read those registries rather than the HIR. hir::lower calls hir::errordecls::hasPayload and the affinity queries hir::types::IsAffine -> hir::structs::IsAffine / hir::enums::IsAffine. Native lowering reads hir::enums::cases, hir::structs::names/fieldTypes, hir::errordecls::payloadType and core::native::metadata, and writes them into the NIR header. Struct types in HIR are nominal ids ({nstruct ID}) whose layout lives in the registry.

Compiling another program between compiling A and running A breaks native for A, and can make the Tcl backends silently compute wrong answers. Compiling a program that only declares a different `type Small` made interp/compile/compile-hir return chk(5)=false, chk(150)=true, where A's own Small (0..10) gives true, false. Native failed (enum key "Light" not known). After a program declaring only an enum: compile-hir and native fail with core::type: unknown type "Small". After one declaring a different struct Point: the compile backend fails with 'struct Point initializer has fields {x y}, but its declaration has {z}'.

claims.claim: The HIR already carries the program's declarations (sourceTypes, errorDecls, errorPayloads, traits), and hir::read shows how to re-register declarations from serialized form. Making backends (or a cache loader) take declarations from the HIR instead of the registries is therefore a plausible way to make HIR self-contained; imports and trait impl tables are not carried.

hir/ is not front-end-only code. Native lowering references about 20 hir namespaces (affine, aot, blockescape, completions, construction, contexts, enums, errordecls, escape, exact, induction, mutvec, range, specialize, stringregion, structs, syscall, traversal, types) and reaches type inference (hir::types::inferRegion) through specialization. The Tcl compiler uses hir::types, hir::affine, hir::aot and hir::completions::BoundsProven. A front end reimplemented in Botlish would leave this code in Tcl for the backends, duplicating type inference, unless the analyses the backends use stayed shared.

summary: The cleanest seam in the front end is the argument list of hir::buildSyntax: syntax-node dicts plus an options dict (-origin, -files, -modules, -imports, -type-decls, -error-decls, -struct-decls, -trait-decls), all plain data (surface/modules.tcl:1097-1111). Everything before that point runs once per program. Everything after it is one indivisible unit, hir::BuildOnce (registry reset, resolve, hygiene, check), which runs many times per program: once per static-decision round, once per method-call trial, once more for trait monomorphization, plus its own inner reruns. The best first step for a Botlish front end is the lexer and parser, which turn text into AST dicts and are pure apart from one core:: call (core::value::isValidScalar). The next step adds lowering and the module loader, emitting buildSyntax's inputs; this needs an exported table of native names and builtin type names. Moving the analyses means moving the whole build loop together: BuildOnce, the static loop with staticdeps, DecideMethodCalls and monomorphize. Otherwise every build costs a cross-language call carrying the HIR in both directions. That is also where the time goes. In four small golden suites, the per-build analysis took about 76-83% of front-end time; parsing took 9-16% (60-75% of that is the lexer, and most of it re-parses lib/test.bot in each fresh process); lowering and loading took 3-6%. Inside a build, hir::types::infer (the type walk plus semantic-instance walks) is the largest single pass at 12-32% of the front end, followed by completions (the errorsets pass), hygiene, affine, mutvec::Elaborate, resolve and semantic::verify. Keeping Tcl as the orchestration language is workable: a Botlish program's result already comes back to Tcl as a host runtime value (native::Outcome), and input can arrive through argv() or stdin, since there is no openat. Compile-once only works inside one process today, and only until another compilation runs. Experiments showed three hidden couplings. First, backends read process-global registries that the front end's last build filled. Second, HIR text cannot round-trip module programs or source origins, and it drops side tables. Third, the Tcl 'compile' backend re-runs hir::build on Core IR, and native lowering reuses hir::types::inferRegion, range, escape and aot from hir/. Other couplings: diagnostics a program can observe include message text, which can contain internal ids and hygiene names, so a reimplementation must reproduce id allocation, walk order and wording exactly. The semantic-instance budget also depends on Tcl's own call depth ([info level] > 700). Language prerequisites I infer for a Botlish front end are a string-keyed map and payload-bearing sum types, since enums are payload-free today.

claims.claim: The pipeline of surface::readProgramFile: load libraries named by '# requires' comments, then compileProgramFile: surface::parse the entry file, then BuildProgram (NewState, then CollectAndLoad: check imports, LoadNamespace recursively (ParseModule, checks, SplitTypeDecls, LowerStatements, RemapFile into a section), CheckRef per qualified reference with static-site deferral), then hir::buildSyntax, then surface::lower::Finish (strict raise plus hir::warnings::run).

The cut at hir::buildSyntax takes only plain data: syntax nodes (dicts {kind origin ...} per hir/syntax.tcl) and an options dict of sections, files, import environments and declaration dicts. No AST is passed beyond this point.

Static decisions work on syntax nodes, not source text: each round Expands the static nodes under the current decisions and calls hir::BuildFull. So a Botlish parser and lowerer that emits syntax (with the 'static' node's body and deferred list) does not interact with the decision loop.

BuildOnce is the unit that is repeated. It resets and refills process-global registries (imports table, errordecls, structs, enums, traits, sourcetypes, which reach core::type and core::native), then runs resolve, hygiene and hir::check (CheckOnce: coroutines, signatures/types, range, callables, lockstep, structs, contexts, affine, mutvec, syscall, semantic, errorsets, modulebinding, opacity, traits). It is called per static round, per method-call trial, and again by traits::monomorphize. check can run CheckOnce twice, and signatures::infer and types::infer loop internally.

Some per-build state is passed through namespace variables instead of arguments: the trait plan and cloneBindings during monomorphization, the semantic-instance run state, affine and completions state, and surface::lower::staticDeferred during lowering. Builds and their passes communicate through process-global state, so individual passes cannot simply be moved across a language boundary.

The backends depend on registries the front end left in the process, so a HIR value is not self-contained. A HIR dict dumped and reloaded in a fresh process runs on interp, but fails on compile (NOT-A-CONTEXT) and on cranelift (unknown type linux::path::LinuxPath). In the building process, compiling an unrelated program first makes cranelift fail on the original HIR with CONTEXT-NATIVE-LOWERING-UNSUPPORTED.

claims.claim: Program-observable outcomes depend on implementation details. A rejected static block becomes CompilerError{code, primary, related, message}, and messages can contain internal ids (block(eN), function eN) and hygiene names (NAME#N) allocated by deterministic per-kind counters in walk order. Some golden tests compare the message text. A reimplementation must therefore reproduce diagnostic order, id allocation, Tcl dict insertion order, lsort order and wording.
The semantic-instance budget depends on Tcl's own call-stack depth ([info level] > levelLimit 700), so an analysis fact depends on the Tcl implementation's recursion depth.

The time is in the per-build analysis. BuildOnce plus BuildFull overhead was about 76-83% of the front end. Parsing was 9-16%, mostly re-parsing library modules (lib/test.bot alone takes about 0.19 s) in each fresh process, and lexing is 60-75% of parse time. Lowering and module loading were 3-6%.

claims.claim: Within a build, hir::types::infer (the type walk including semantic-instance walks) is the largest pass: about 12% (traits-path), 19% (representation), 21% (errors) and 23-32% (loops) of the whole front end. Next come completions (the errorsets row), hygiene (0.37-0.48 s for 2-3 builds), affine, mutvec::Elaborate (which runs per BuildFull, so per round), resolve and semantic::verify.

Hygiene exists only for consumers that identify bindings by name (Core IR, the Tcl compiler, HIR text); the native path does not need it. It still runs in every BuildOnce, including discarded trial builds.

The number of builds multiplies the cost: the small suites measured took 2-3 builds, but the economics report lists mutable-vector.bot at 30 builds, mutable-array.bot at 21 and structs-and-enums.bot at 19.

Tcl can stay the orchestrator. A native run returns the program's value rendered as host runtime values, which native::Outcome reads directly. Botlish input is available through argv() on all backends and through read(2) on stdin under Linux native; there is no openat.

Language prerequisites for a Botlish front end: enums are payload-free, so heterogeneous AST and HIR nodes need another encoding, and there is no built-in map type. HIR entity ids are dense per-kind counters, so the core tables could be vectors, but name-keyed registries need maps.

Module ASTs are cached only inside one process, keyed by file text. Lowered module sections are not directly reusable across programs because FileIds are assigned in load order and remapped. A cross-process AST cache would be a cheap form of compile-once for libraries.

summary:
Yes, Tcl can stay the orchestrator, but only across a process boundary. Today Tcl never calls Botlish code in-process. native::evalHir lowers HIR to NIR in Tcl, writes it to a temp file, starts the botlish-native process for each run, and parses one `value`/`error` line from its stdout. AOT executables are separate ELF binaries that print the program's final value and exit 0, or exit 1 on a run-time failure.

Getting source in works today only through argv():
- JIT path: a hex-encoded --argv-file has no size limit. A 1 MB argument went through intact, astral characters included. Arguments must be strict UTF-8, and NUL is refused by the Tcl injection layer.
- AOT path: real argv, at most 131071 bytes per argument (verified) and about 2 MB in total.
- stdin and files cannot be used for text. linux::io::read returns MutableBytes, but abi::bytes deliberately has no indexing or decoding, no native turns bytes into a String, and there is no openat wrapper.

Getting output back:
- Best: one top-level String result. The protocol escapes about 4 characters per space or newline.
- Avoid nested results. Escaping doubles with each nesting level: 16 characters per space inside a List[String], and a 3-level list returned 46.9x its size.
- Alternative: AOT stdout via io::print. In the JIT path, io::print output is mixed into the protocol pipe and native::evalHir throws it away.

Deployment should be an AOT executable (2-4 ms start-up, about 0.7-0.8 s to link). evalHir repeats the Tcl HIR-to-NIR lowering on every call: 0.5 s for traits-path and 1.0 s for representation, about 20x the Cranelift time. AOT requires every used specialized instance to be closed (fully typed). The golden suites with lib/test.bot are closed, but the untyped examples/stdlib/hashtable.bot has 4 guarded regions, so a Botlish compiler must be written typed.

Diagnostics have to be data. There is no exit-status facility, and an unhandled declared error at top level is a compile error. A run-time failure shows up as `error {CODE} MSG` (JIT) or as exit 1 plus a stderr line (AOT, including NATIVE LIMIT STACK). Recursion is not a problem: 10^7 non-tail frames ran fine, and 10^8 failed cleanly.

The real coupling is the format the Botlish front end would hand back. The Tcl backends consume an in-memory HIR dict with about 31 top-level tables and side tables, and native/lower.tcl calls dozens of hir/ analyses (range, specialize, escape, aot, affine releases, types, contexts). HIR text (hir::format/hir::parse) is a debugging format: it fails on any program that imports a module, and it drops 9 side tables (affine, contexts, coroutines, mutvec, semantic, method decisions, flagAllowed). The full dict printed as text is 1.38 MB for traits-path, half of it traitSource. So a Botlish front end must either emit that dict, or a new complete interchange format has to be built, or the Botlish part stops at an earlier boundary such as the AST. But parsing is only about 14% of front-end time for traits-path (271 of 1890 ms); signatures, errorsets, static decisions and affine are larger.

What a compiler written in Botlish would lean on:
- Present: structs (recursive types allowed), payload-free enums, error payloads, static traits, typed MutableVector/MutableArray (good for dense integer ids), closures, `hash`.
- Strings: concat (linear only thanks to virtual-construction plans; quadratic with them off), substring, length, and char_at (O(1) on ASCII Strings, but it decodes from the start on any non-ASCII String: 187 vs 38 ms at 20K characters).
- Missing or limited:
  - Maps: no map or dict type. ImmutableSet has only from_list and contains, with O(n) membership. Hash tables have to be hand-written and typed to stay AOT-ready.
  - Strings: no String ordering (`<` is Int-only), no character-to-String, Int-to-String or String-to-Int conversion, no String iteration, no character classifiers, no bytes-to-String decoding.
  - Types: no type variables or user-defined generic types, no enum payloads or `match`.
  - Process: no file I/O and no exit status.

summary: The most expensive part of the front end is the type-inference core that runs inside every build. hir::signatures::infer drives hir::types::infer, which also drives the opportunistic semantic instances (hir::semantic::Call/Analyze/Walk), and hir::semantic::verify re-checks those instances. The bench's 'signatures' phase is mostly this whole-program type walk, not contract solving, because hir::types::infer and the instance walks are not in the profiled phase list and so count toward it. On representation.bot, signatures::infer took 844 ms inclusive: 420 ms generic typing walk, 283 ms instance walks, about 124 ms requirement collection, solving and installation. Each checked build does at least two full typings. The second signature round only confirms the trusted contracts and costs about as much as the first (254+192 ms and 120+142 ms on representation.bot); even a program that only imports compiler and test needs both. The time that grows faster than program size is the semantic-instance layer. On a generated program, front end 0.79/1.91/8.65/38.3 s at 25/50/100/200 units with instances on, and 0.95/2.13/4.39 s at 50/100/200 with them off, which is linear. The reason is O(program) work per instance: semantic::Walk analyzes over a copy-on-write copy of the whole HIR, semantic::View copies the HIR and re-interns types again for verification, and verify and End scan lists, costing O(instances x calls). Instances grow with the program, so the total is about quadratic. That fits destructuring.bot (15k HIR expressions), where signatures 39% plus semantic-instances 14.5% dominate. Next come avoidable whole-program rescans repeated in every build: hygiene renames each module definition with a scan of every expression (errors.bot: 153 renames, 524 ms, 10%), and hir::contexts::Walk rebuilds the same parent maps about 10 times per build (representation.bot: 298 ms, 9%). The bench's 'static-decisions' phase is mostly not decision logic: it is per-build elaboration (mutvec::Elaborate, traits::Stamp) that BuildFull runs. Work done once per program (parse, module loading, surface lowering) is 13-34% of the small suites I measured but about 1-2% of large ones. Everything else is paid on each of the 329 builds, including re-analyzing about 1450 HIR expressions of lib/test.bot, lib/compiler.bot and their imports in every build (about 0.5 s each). Parsing, surface lowering and the decision scheduler are cleanly separable but cheap. The hot typing core shares one mutable HIR dict and per-compilation global registries with about 12k lines of tightly coupled analyses, so it can only be split off as a whole build (syntax in, HIR out). The quadratic, per-build and per-round costs are algorithmic and would stay in any language; the roughly 0.65 µs to read a node field and about 40 µs per expression per walk are Tcl overhead that compiled code would cut by a large constant factor.

Could intermediate decision builds skip mutvec::Elaborate, ElaborateResumes and Stamp, since Attribute only reads diagnostics? Elaborate's body (hir/mutvec.tcl:369-596) records no diagnostic, but staticdeps::Deps reads that round's HIR, so this needs checking.

Could hygiene run once on the final HIR, or be indexed (binding -> its refs)? Some messages print binding names (the known hygiene-name gap in STATIC-DECISION-ECONOMICS.md), so diagnostic wording must be checked first.

For compile-once across processes, or a frontend written in Botlish with Tcl still orchestrating: hir::format does not print the 'semantic' side table, and hir/specialize.tcl:1014 reads it for precision. Does the HIR text round trip carry everything the backends use, or would a reader need to re-run hir::check?

lib/ has no hash-map type (only lists, ImmutableSet, MutableVector/MutableArray). A Botlish front end would need maps or dense-id arrays to avoid the same per-node lookup and copying costs. Which language milestone would supply that?

Could analysis summaries of library modules (lib/test.bot, lib/compiler.bot) be cached across builds and suites? Instances are keyed by caller argument types, and trait/affine monomorphization clones module functions, so only the caller-independent parts look cacheable.

verdicts.claim: hir::read is designed as the inverse of hir::format: it rebuilds a complete HIR and trusts the printed facts without re-deriving them.
verdicts.evidence: Verified by reading. The design intent is as claimed: hir/read.tcl:1-20, the calleeErrors placeholder at hir/read.tcl:1004-1011, handlerTypes set to any at hir/read.tcl:1281-1282, and compiler/compiler.tcl:171-173. 'Complete' does not hold for backends. hir::read::Program (hir/read.tcl:352-407) does not rebuild the `coroutines` protocol table or the `semantic` table, and both are read during native lowering (see claims 3, 8 and 9). Diffing fields on traits-path also showed traitClone and traitImpl coming back in a reduced form (traitImpl without `impl`), and inferredResultType set from the printed block type (hir/read.tcl:961). No backend reads those three.

verdicts.claim: The format prints declarations, then only the entry program's top scope header and the root expressions. Module section scopes are never printed.
verdicts.evidence: Read hir/format.tcl:72-103, 226-235 and hir/read.tcl:362-378. One detail: the module sections' root expressions (including their `bind` lines) are printed, flattened under the entry program's header with no scope. Running main's format on examples/surface/14-modules.bot gives `program s2` followed by `e1 bind b1 mathish::inc`, although e1's scope is s3. Blocks also print `staticRefs (...)` (hir/format.tcl:351-352), and the reader reads it back (hir/read.tcl:905).

verdicts.claim: Backend-facing analysis facts are deliberately printed and read back with fallbacks: affine moves and releases, contexts, trait clones, coroutine effect and resume, proofs, declared errors, known.
verdicts.evidence: Verified: the affine flags (hir/format.tcl:248-320 and hir/read.tcl:800-830), the accessor fallbacks (hir/affine.tcl:1708-1769) and context installs (hir/contexts.tcl:407-412) work as claimed. Missing from the list: the coroutine protocol table. The block's `coroutine-effect` text (hir/format.tcl:405-410) does not restore it. hir::coroutines::ShapeResult (hir/coroutines.tcl:541-545) returns `any` when `coroutines` is absent, and it runs during the specializer's re-inference. Experiment: a 12-line module-free coroutine program gets an extra `guard coroutine %2 "coroutine#start"` in its specialized NIR after a real format/parse round trip. Values are unchanged.

verdicts.claim: A program with source-module imports does not read back, and the repository's tests acknowledge this.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced: traits-path fails with 'HIR text line 20: binding b1 (linux::path::nul_free?) is not declared and is not a root name', and 14-modules.bot fails at line 2 (mathish::inc). The error comes from hir/read.tcl:543-545, and the module scopes come from hir/resolve.tcl:111-114 and 141-155. The tests say so at tests/error-payloads.test:349, tests/immutable-set.test:46-50 and tests/loop-collecting.test:582. Scale: 21 of 41 examples/*/*.bot plus bench/*.bot programs import a source module.

verdicts.claim: Both backends need module identity from HIR tables the text lacks.
verdicts.evidence: Read compiler/compiler.tcl:185-194 and 605-620, native/lower.tcl:1788-1792, 5012 and 5224, and hir/hir.tcl:1195-1203 (hir::isModuleBinding reads moduleScopeIds).

verdicts.claim: For module-free programs the round trip is semantically exact: Core IR, specialized and generic NIR identical except where boundsVerdicts matter.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced on ai_text_clean.bot: Core IR identical, and the only NIR difference is one strcharatproven→strcharat line in both specialized and generic NIR. Refuted for coroutine programs: a module-free program (fn gen(xs) loop/yield; drive() with `coroutine {step, first} = gen(xs)`) had identical Core IR and identical generic NIR, but its specialized NIR differed by 17 lines, starting with an added `guard coroutine ... "coroutine#start"`. Cause: the `coroutines` table is not rebuilt (hir/coroutines.tcl:541-545). Values were identical on interp, cranelift and cranelift-generic.

verdicts.claim: boundsVerdicts is not printed. After read-back BoundsProven returns 0, so proven bounds checks are kept. This costs performance, not correctness.
verdicts.evidence: Neither hir/format.tcl nor hir/read.tcl mentions boundsVerdicts. hir/completions.tcl:3591-3602 returns 0 without verdicts. Consumers: native/lower.tcl:6091, 6551, 7422 and 7452, and compiler/compiler.tcl:1258. Reproduced the ai_text_clean strcharatproven→strcharat difference with identical values.

verdicts.claim: In 4 golden suites, stripping every unprinted per-node and table fact except boundsVerdicts left NIR byte-identical.
verdicts.evidence: The simulation left out an unprinted table that read-back loses: `coroutines`. On traits-path, removing only that table (with semantic and boundsVerdicts already stripped) adds 3 lines to specialized NIR: `guard coroutine %1 "coroutine#start" @e1319`, `guard list %2 "loop" @e1326` and `guard list %22 "loop" @e1342`. I also simulated a module-aware read-back of traits-path by copying only scope structure into hir::parse output. Its specialized NIR differs from the semantic+bounds-stripped NIR by exactly those 3 guards, and its generic NIR matches. Stripping `semantic` also changes NIR elsewhere (claim 9). Removing contexts, mutvec, traitSource, methodCalls or flagAllowed one at a time changed nothing.

verdicts.claim: The specializer and range analysis read the semantic-instance table and inferred trusted parameter contracts, but in tested programs these did not change NIR.
verdicts.evidence: True for inferredParamTypes, checkedParamTypes, paramRequirements and paramNotes: stripping them changed no NIR in any program I tried (traits-path, csv_records, hashtable, opaque-instances, a MutableArray probe). False for `semantic`, which is read at hir/specialize.tcl:1014 via hir/semantic.tcl:695-701. (a) examples/stdlib/csv_records.bot with only `semantic` removed: specialized native lowering throws NATIVE UNSUPPORTED struct-shape at csv_records.bot:357:23 ('.values' has a receiver of type any). The original compiles and runs natively. (b) A 14-line program with a generic fn over MutableArray gains a `guard int` in specialized NIR without `semantic`. So losing semantic instances can make a natively compilable program fail native compilation, not only cost speed.

verdicts.claim: Source spans and the files table do not survive. `-origins 1` text of a source HIR fails to parse, and backend messages lose file:line.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced on 15-enums: 'HIR text line 4: origin file f1 does not match its position (ir 0)'. The files table is empty after read-back, and an origin like {file f1 ... line 18 column 8} becomes {ir {0 2 2 1}}. Code: hir/read.tcl:691-695 and 793-796, and the fallback in hir/aot.tcl:912-926. A read-back NATIVE UNSUPPORTED error printed 'ir {2 2 2 2}' instead of 'hof.bot:11:5'.

Reproduced 'HIR text line 3: not a list of words' for "line1
line2", "ab
" and "a
# not a comment". These round-trip with equal interp and native values: , {, }{, quotes, #x, ' : ' with @, backslash, trailing spaces, tab, and [x]$y. The newline literal also appears in lib/io.bot:59 and :67 and in 11 golden suites (e.g. tests/golden/contexts.bot:559 and bits-bytes-hashing.bot:436).

verdicts.claim: The in-memory HIR is not self-contained: once another program is compiled in the same process, native lowering of the first HIR fails.
verdicts.evidence: The coupling is confirmed, but the failure can be silent. I compiled a struct program (Record), then 15-enums.bot, then ran native::nir on the first HIR again. It raised no error. The NIR changed: `%4 = op listnew ...; ret %4` became `unreachable @e17`, and native::evalHir failed at run time with 'native code reached a point HIR proved unreachable (function total)'. Interp is unaffected. Reading a text also invalidates other live HIRs: after hir::parse of the struct program's text, 15-enums' in-memory HIR failed natively with 'key "Light" not known in dictionary', because hir::enums::Reset runs unconditionally at hir/read.tcl:87. hir/sourcetypes.tcl:24-71 documents this limitation ('not built for concurrent or nested compilation').

verdicts.claim: Reading HIR text re-establishes the registries from the declarations in the text, the same path a source compile uses.
verdicts.evidence: Only for the kinds of declaration the text contains. Enums are always reset (hir/read.tcl:87). Source types, structs, traits and errors are applied only when present (hir/read.tcl:103-105, 115-141, 156-164 and 339-342). Experiment: after reading 15-enums' text (no structs), hir::structs::declared Record from an earlier program still returned 1. Errors leak even on a source compile: hir::errordecls::apply returns the previous `current` for empty decls (hir/errordecls.tcl:169-173). A source compile of 15-enums after a program declaring `error Boom` produced errorDecls 'Boom', and its hir::format text contained an `error Boom` line.

verdicts.claim: No backend reads these omitted tables: warnings, static*, method*, flagAllowed, traitSource. violatedDeclared exists only in -strict 0 HIR.
verdicts.evidence: Grepped native/*.tcl, compiler/compiler.tcl, hir/lower.tcl, specialize, range, escape, aot, blockescape, stringregion, traversal and construction. The only hits outside report scripts are violatedDeclared in native/prepare.tcl:31-58 and hir/range.tcl. demotedContracts is read only by hir/static.tcl:1203. The list leaves out `semantic` and `coroutines`, which backends do read (claims 3 and 9).

verdicts.evidence: Read hir/hir.tcl:398-404 (hir::static::decide on $nodes), 439-447 (DecideMethodCalls, and traits::monomorphize given $nodes and $syntax) and 448-462. hir::check (hir/hir.tcl:878-915) can run CheckOnce twice. verdicts.evidence: Read main.tcl:118-123 and compiler/compiler.tcl:151-160 and 582-584 (hir::build $exprs -mode $mode -strict 0 when no HIR is given). The golden runner's default backend list (tests/golden/run.tcl:202) uses the Core-IR `compile` path (run.tcl:93-97).
