verdicts.evidence: traits-path: format 27 ms, 125,181 chars (same size as claimed), against a 1668 ms front end. ai_text_clean: format 4 ms and parse 33 ms against a 174 ms front end (19%). On very small programs reading is a larger share: hof.bot 13/51 ms, co.bot 22/64 ms.

verdicts.claim: Adding module sections to the format looks like a contained, mechanical extension.
verdicts.evidence: I tested this by simulation, not by implementing it. I declared the module sections' local bindings in the header, ran hir::parse, then copied only the section scopes, scope parents, expression scopes, modules and moduleScopeIds from the source HIR. traits-path then read back with identical Core IR, identical types for every expression and binding, and the same report on cranelift and compile-hir ('2 passed, 0 failed'). The NIR still differed, and only through unprinted facts: boundsVerdicts, plus the 3 guards from the coroutines table. Not tested: the 11 golden suites with newline literals, and real section headers in the reader.

verdicts.claim: A Botlish front end would also need the Tcl native registry's metadata (92 natives), which front-end analyses read heavily.
verdicts.evidence: core::native::metadata appears 45 times in hir/ and surface/, and core::native::names returns 92. The front end also writes into the global core registries: source types register constructors and predicates (hir/sourcetypes.tcl:510-516) and unregister them on reset (hir/sourcetypes.tcl:80-90). The text reader re-applies these.

missed: NATIVE-BOTLISH-LOWERING-IMPL.md (status: analysis only) already covers much of this question. §3 says 'hir::format/hir::parse are debugging formats' and lists what they leave out: module sections, `semantic`, violatedDeclared/demotedContracts, and the completions and lockstep stamps. It proposes a dedicated 'lowering input' (dense ids, per-instance overlays, precomputed Tcl-only facts), checked by byte-identical NIR. §1 measured csv_records: front end 833 ms (50%), hir analyses inside native::lowered 659 ms (40%). §9 suggests cutting after hir::check and notes the front end grows superlinearly (62 s for a 7.2k-line program).

The native backend re-runs the front end's type inference. hir::specialize calls hir::types::inferRegion (hir/specialize.tcl:814 and 1519), and native lowering runs the specialize, range, escape, stringregion, blockescape, traversal and construction analyses itself (native/lower.tcl:1412-1444). So the Tcl inference engine cannot be dropped behind a Botlish front end, and the Botlish front end's facts must agree with Tcl's re-inference. This is how the unprinted `coroutines` (hir/coroutines.tcl:541-545) and `semantic` (hir/specialize.tcl:1014) tables reach the NIR.

Tcl-side native lowering costs about as much as the front end, so a Botlish front end does not make compile-once cheap. traits-path: native::nir 551-608 ms specialized plus 254-284 ms generic, against a 1.5-1.9 s front end. harness: 1101 ms plus 550 ms, against 1617 ms. golden run.tcl lowers each suite to NIR twice: generic and specialized.

Counterexample: losing `semantic` turns a working native compile into NATIVE UNSUPPORTED struct-shape. examples/stdlib/csv_records.bot:357:23 fails when only the semantic table is removed. A text format would also have to carry `semantic` and `coroutines`, not just module sections, newline-safe literals and boundsVerdicts.

The registry coupling can fail silently. Native lowering of a still-valid in-memory HIR, after another compile in the same process, emitted `unreachable` in place of the program's result with no lowering error. Separately, error declarations leak from one compilation into the next program's HIR and HIR text (hir/errordecls.tcl:169-173; hir/hir.tcl BuildOnce stores the result as errorDecls).

Compile-once opportunity that needs no Botlish rewrite: library modules are re-parsed and re-analyzed for every program. lib/test.bot alone takes 176 of 233 ms of traits-path's parse time, and every golden suite imports it. Caching library ASTs or analyzed sections would cut the 'syntax' share.

The golden runner's default `compile` backend is not compile-once. tests/golden/run.tcl:202 and 93-97 run Core IR through core::compiler, which calls hir::build again (compiler/compiler.tcl:582-584). The compile-hir path, which reuses the HIR, is opt-in.

Limits relevant to a large Botlish front end, from NATIVE-BOTLISH-LOWERING-IMPL.md §1 and §9 (not re-measured): the front end overflows Tcl nesting in hir::completions at a static call depth of about 110 (2,000-line synthetic chain), and the specializer and semantic-instance budgets are 8/1000 and 16/2000.

verdicts.claim: The golden runner compiles each suite once (surface::readProgramFile -warnings off) and runs the one HIR on every backend (hir::lower + core::evalProgram for interp/compile, core::compiler::evalHir for compile-hir, native::evalHir with -specialize 0 for cranelift-generic).
verdicts.evidence: I read tests/golden/run.tcl:64-71 (golden::compile), 86-101 (golden::run) and 173-183 (one compile, then a loop over the backends). Two qualifications. compile-hir runs only when asked for: the default list at run.tcl:202 is interp, compile, cranelift-generic, cranelift. And the 'compile' backend does not compile the front end's HIR: it compiles an HIR it rebuilds from Core IR (see the compile-backend claim below).

verdicts.claim: Within one compilation, backends do not interfere: NIR (specialized and generic) and Core IR regenerated after running other backends are identical.
verdicts.evidence: I reproduced it on tests/golden/traits-path.bot: native::nir, native::nir -specialize 0 and hir::lower, then the compile, interp and compile-hir backends, then all three again gave 'nir same 1 generic same 1 coreir same 1'. This holds only because the compile backend's rebuild (hir::build of Core IR) passes no -struct-decls/-type-decls/-trait-decls, and hir::errordecls::apply {} keeps the current registry (hir/errordecls.tcl:169-174), so the registries survive that rebuild.

verdicts.claim: The front end fills process-wide registries that are not part of the HIR value (imports, errordecls, structs, enums, traits, sourcetypes into core::type/core::native), all from hir::BuildOnce.
verdicts.evidence: I read hir/hir.tcl:471-543 (BuildOnce). A namespace-variable diff around the traits-path front end showed changes to hir::enums::registry, hir::structs::{registry,affinity}, hir::errordecls::{payloads,current}, hir::sourcetypes::generation, hir::imports::table, hir::traits::{unitNames,impls,registry} and core::type::registry. core/type.tcl:444-456 (definePredicate) registers predicate natives into core::native. Qualification: much of this content is also in the HIR. sourceTypes carries enum and struct entries with fields, opaque and context flags (the test::Suite entry has 'context 1'). The backends just do not read it from there.

verdicts.claim: The backends read those registries rather than the HIR (hir::lower via errordecls::hasPayload and IsAffine; native lowering via enums::cases, structs::names/fieldTypes, errordecls, core::native::metadata, written into the NIR header).
verdicts.evidence: Code read: hir/lower.tcl:337, hir/types.tcl:492-498 (IsAffine goes to hir::structs/hir::enums), 685-704 (StructLayout/StructField read hir::structs for a nominal struct), native/lower.tcl:1551-1576 (header built from core::native::metadata, hir::structs::isOpaque, hir::enums::cases) and 3700-3722 (EnumIndex/EnumConst). The Tcl interp runtime also reads the registry while it runs: a source predicate is core::type::PredicateImpl, which calls validate against core::type::registry (core/type.tcl:444-461). That is why its wrong answers are silent.

verdicts.claim: Compiling another program between compiling A and running A breaks native for A and can make the Tcl backends silently compute wrong answers.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced, one fresh process per variant. With A = type Small 0..10, enum, struct, chk(n)=Small?(n), compiling B 'type Small = Int in 100..200' made interp, compile and compile-hir return [false, true, ...] for A instead of [true, false, ...]. After B 'struct Point: z: int', compile failed with 'struct Point initializer has fields {x y}, but its declaration has {z}'. The effect is stronger than claimed: compiling the declaration-free program '1 + 2' between compiling A0 (enum, struct, payload error) and running it also broke native. cranelift-generic failed with TCL LOOKUP DICT Point, and specialized cranelift built code that trapped at run time with NATIVE BUG 'native code reached a point HIR proved unreachable'. The interp, compile and compile-hir backends stayed correct. Cause: every surface compile passes -struct-decls and -type-decls, so hir::structs::Reset and hir::enums::Reset run even when the program declares nothing (hir/hir.tcl:481-492).

verdicts.claim: The golden 'compile' backend calls back into the front end (compileUnit -> GenerateUnit -> hir::build, re-running resolution, hygiene and hir::check); core::compiler::evalHir (main.tcl's compile path) skips it.
verdicts.evidence: The golden part is confirmed. Code: compiler/compiler.tcl:151-161 and 582-589 ('hir::build $exprs -mode $mode -strict 0'). A trace of the compile backend on traits-path counted hir::build=1, BuildOnce=1, hir::check=1 and signatures::infer=1, taking 0.84 s against a 1.63 s front end. compile-hir showed none of these. The main.tcl part is wrong: its -backend compile path does rebuild. main.tcl:111-112 lowers to Core IR, which evalHir then lowers again (compiler.tcl:178). After the run, main.tcl:183-186 calls core::compiler::programTypes $program, which goes compiler.tcl:223 -> Cached -> compileUnit -> GenerateUnit -> hir::build. Replaying those steps on a small program counted hir::lower 2, GenerateUnit 2, hir::build 1, BuildOnce 1, hir::check 1.

verdicts.claim: The native backend never calls surface::*, hir::buildSyntax/BuildFull, the static decisions or warnings; its only re-check is native::prepareHir's hir::check, run only for violatedDeclared, which a strict HIR never has.
verdicts.evidence: Grep of native/*.tcl: surface:: appears only at native/native.tcl:95, a source guard. hir::build appears only in the tools native/explain-native.tcl:67 and generate-post-stack-details.tcl:20. I read native/prepare.tcl:27-58. With hir::check, buildSyntax, BuildOnce, static::decide and warnings::run wrapped, the cranelift and cranelift-generic runs on traits-path called none of them. A strict compile raises any diagnostic (surface/lower.tcl:275-283). Every violatedDeclared write comes with a Diagnose (hir/range.tcl:1670-1700), so a returned strict HIR has none. DIRECT-HIR-NATIVE-PATH.md:186-190 still describes the removed module-implementation re-check; the doc is stale.

verdicts.claim: Each native run does its own native-only analyses (specialize with per-instance inferRegion, range, rawabi, escape, stringregion, blockescape, traversal, construction, shortstr), and these dominate native time over NIR emission and the Rust driver.
verdicts.evidence: I read native/lower.tcl:1409-1470 and hir/specialize.tcl:814 and 1519 (inferRegion). Trace on traits-path, specialized: native::lower::program 0.54 s inclusive (specialize::analyze 0.26 s, range 0.09 s, inferRegion 128 calls) against native::Driver 0.04 s. Generic: lower::program 0.33 s against Driver 0.04 s. I did not check the analysis/NIR split for harness and errors.

verdicts.claim: native::executable runs hir::specialize::analyze twice (readiness check, then inside native::nir).
verdicts.evidence: Code read. native/native.tcl:270 calls hir::specialize::analyze. native.tcl:288 then calls nir, which goes through lowered and native::lower::program to the second analyze at native/lower.tcl:1409. I did not reproduce the timings (0.68 s total, 0.63 s link).

verdicts.claim: hir::lower is quadratic (Pending calls hir::affine::temporaries, which walks all exprs, per call/struct node) and dominates the interp backend; the Tcl compiler and native lowering compute temporaries once per program.
verdicts.evidence: The quadratic part is confirmed. hir/lower.tcl:72, 101, 167 and 357 call temporaries, and hir/affine.tcl:1774-1815 iterates every expr. On traits-path interp, one hir::lower made 322 temporaries calls: 0.29 s of hir::lower's 0.30 s, out of a 0.335 s backend. The Tcl compiler part is wrong. GenerateUnit computes temporaries once (compiler.tcl:596), but CompileBlock calls hir::lower::params/body for every block expression (compiler.tcl:669) to embed its Core IR, which re-enters Pending. compile-hir made 718 temporaries calls taking 0.67 s of its 0.80 s; the compile backend made 719 calls, 1.02 s of 2.0 s. Native does compute it once (native/lower.tcl:1362; 1 call in the trace).

verdicts.claim: Front-end cost by phase on small suites: type inference is the largest (14-18%), parse next, then errorsets, hygiene, semantic instances, mutvec elaboration, affine; static rounds 1/2/3 with 2/2/3 builds.
verdicts.evidence: Magnitudes reproduced on traits-path (front end 1.65 s): signatures::infer 0.311 s inclusive (18.9%), surface::parse 0.245 s (14.9%), errorsets 0.162, affine 0.141, mutvec::Elaborate 0.118, resolve 0.088, hygiene 0.072. On harness: parse 0.307 s against signatures::infer 0.298 s. The investigation's own numbers say parse is larger on two of three suites (0.30 vs 0.24, 0.32 vs 0.25), so 'type inference is the largest, parse next' does not hold in a cold process. There parse ties with or exceeds type inference, mostly from library modules. Also, traits-path's second build is not a static round. It is the trait monomorphization, a full second BuildOnce (hir/hir.tcl:443-447): hir::traits::monomorphize took 0.557 s, 34% of the front end.

verdicts.claim: On large suites static-compile rounds multiply cost (destructuring.bot 306.7 s front end: signatures 39%, static-deps 14.5%, semantic instances 14.5%, hygiene 9%, parse 1.2%; Core IR lowering 135 s vs interp run 3 s); repo report quotes about 900 s and 1600 s for mutable-vector.bot and mutable-array.bot.
verdicts.evidence: Not reproduced (over the time budget). I checked that the sources say what is quoted. scratchpad bench1.txt (mtime Oct 12 05:41) lists these exact figures. STATIC-DECISION-ECONOMICS.md:266-270 gives 904.4/897.7 s and 1620.3/1590.8 s. hir/static.tcl:1308-1326 confirms each round is a full hir::BuildFull. Several hir/staticdeps commits landed after bench1.txt was written, so those numbers may be stale.

verdicts.claim: Caching works across processes if the HIR dict string is stored with a registry snapshot; with HIR alone only interp (and sometimes compile-hir) passes; load is milliseconds; HIR about 1 MB, registries about 70 KB.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced for traits-path with 12 registry variables: all 5 backends passed in a fresh process, load took 7-8 ms, the HIR was 1,378,194 bytes and the registries 69,170 bytes. With HIR only: interp passed, compile failed with NOT-A-CONTEXT, and compile-hir and both native backends failed with 'unknown type linux::path::LinuxPath'. For my module-free a0 program, HIR only passed interp, compile and compile-hir; native failed. About half of traits-path's HIR string is traitSource (690 KB), a complete embedded copy of the pre-monomorphization HIR that no backend reads (hir/traits.tcl:2281-2284).

verdicts.claim: The HIR text format (hir::format/hir::parse) does not work as a cache format: traits-path fails to read back, and it omits the semantic side table by design.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced. Text formatted with the registries loaded failed to parse in a fresh process: 'HIR text line 20: binding b1 (linux::path::nul_free?) is not declared and is not a root name'. The module-free a0 program round-trips and passes all 5 backends. hir/hir.tcl:68-82 documents that warnings and semantic are not printed. hir::format itself also depends on the registries: in a fresh process without them it fails with 'core::type: unknown type "linux::path::LinuxPath"'.

verdicts.claim: The HIR already carries the program's declarations (sourceTypes, errorDecls, errorPayloads, traits), hir::read shows how to re-register them, so backends could take them from the HIR; imports and trait impl tables are not carried.
verdicts.evidence: The facts check out. traits-path's HIR keys include sourceTypes (with enum and struct entries, including the context flag), errorDecls, errorPayloads and traits, but no imports or impls table. hir/read.tcl:77-130 re-registers through hir::sourcetypes::apply and hir::structs::applyEntries. Qualification: the HIR's errorDecls/errorPayloads can be stale. A program with no error declarations compiled after one with errors carries the earlier program's: '1 + 2' compiled after a0 had errorDecls={Boom} (hir/errordecls.tcl:169-174 returns the previous 'current'). Taking declarations from the HIR is still my inference and was not tried.

verdicts.claim: hir/ is not front-end-only: native lowering references about 20 hir namespaces and reaches type inference via specialization; the Tcl compiler uses hir::types, affine, aot, completions::BoundsProven; a Botlish front end would leave this in Tcl or duplicate it.
verdicts.evidence: Grep of native/{lower,rawabi,shortstring,prepare,native}.tcl found 19 hir::X:: namespaces: range 70, escape 57, specialize 55, types 42, aot 37, ... completions 1. compiler/compiler.tcl uses hir::affine, types, lower, aot, mutvec and completions. hir/specialize.tcl:814 and 1519 call hir::types::inferRegion, 1014 calls hir::semantic::GenericResult, and 1972 calls hir::resolve::nativeSymbol. The conclusion about duplication is inference.

verdicts.claim: NIR is a deterministic, self-contained text artifact (header carries natives' metadata, shapes, enum tables; the driver receives only the text plus argv); caching NIR would skip the native analyses.
verdicts.evidence: native::nir of traits-path in two separate processes gave the same md5. Passing the NIR text straight to native::Driver run produced the suite's report ('2 passed, 0 failed'). native/native.tcl:149-185 writes only the NIR and argv files. Qualification: the NIR depends on BOTLISH_NATIVE_* environment variables read at lowering time (native/lower.tcl:1260-1280 and the struct-width variables at 1381-1395), so a cache key must include them.

verdicts.claim: Loading the Tcl compiler sources is negligible (0.046 s), so running the front end in a separate process costs little beyond (de)serializing about 1 MB of HIR.
verdicts.evidence: Sourcing compiler, surface and native measured 0.0466 s. But a fresh front-end process also loses the per-process module parse cache (surface/modules.tcl:119-145): parse costs 0.25-0.31 s per cold compile on traits-path and harness, mostly library modules (traits-path's own file is 73 lines). A short-lived front-end process pays that every time, while a long-lived one runs into the registry leaks.

missed: Front-end isolation is broken, not just backend isolation. hir::errordecls::apply keeps the previous program's errors when a program declares none (hir/errordecls.tcl:169-174), and hir::sourcetypes::apply keeps earlier source types and predicate natives registered (hir/sourcetypes.tcl:121-138). Experiments: a program that fails with an undeclared 'Boom' is rejected when compiled fresh ('unknown error "Boom"'). Compiled in the same process after a program declaring Boom, it compiles and runs ([0, 1007] on interp and cranelift). A program calling an undeclared Small? is rejected fresh ('unbound name "Small?"') but compiles and runs after a program declaring Small. So HIR is not a pure function of the source in a long-lived process. That matters for a compile cache or a Tcl orchestrator that compiles many programs.

Any surface compile resets the struct and enum registries, even one declaring nothing (hir/hir.tcl:481-492: surface always passes -struct-decls and -type-decls). Compiling '1 + 2' after A0 and before running A0 made specialized cranelift miscompile A0: a run-time trap, NATIVE BUG 'native code reached a point HIR proved unreachable'. This is not a clean lowering error.

The Tcl compiler re-enters the quadratic hir::lower once per block expression. CompileBlock calls hir::lower::params/body (compiler/compiler.tcl:669). On traits-path compile-hir made 718 hir::affine::temporaries calls, taking 0.67 s of the 0.80 s backend.

main.tcl -backend compile lowers twice (main.tcl:111-112, then compiler/compiler.tcl:178). After the run it calls core::compiler::programTypes $program (main.tcl:183-186), which goes compiler.tcl:223 -> compileUnit -> GenerateUnit -> hir::build at compiler.tcl:588. That repeats a whole BuildOnce + hir::check and a second code generation just to print types.

Trait monomorphization is a full second whole-program build (hir/hir.tcl:443-447, hir::traits::monomorphize at hir/traits.tcl:2250). On traits-path it took 0.557 s, 34% of the front end. It runs whenever any loaded module declares a trait (lib/io.bot, lib/io/path.bot), or for the affine plan of coroutine-using programs (hir/hir.tcl:430-431). It is a separable front-end cost the investigation counted as 'builds'.

The final HIR embeds the whole pre-monomorphization HIR as traitSource (hir/traits.tcl:2281-2284; 690 KB of traits-path's 1.38 MB). Only hir/contexts.tcl:1124 and hir/warnings.tcl:137 read it, never a backend, so a cache or front-end seam could drop half the payload.

hir::format, the HIR's own text printer, depends on the registries: in a fresh process without them it fails with 'core::type: unknown type "linux::path::LinuxPath"'. Even the documented textual interface is registry-coupled.

The front end reads Tcl-registered native metadata: 92 natives at startup, each with paramTypes, resultType, ownership, completion, errors, bounds, resultRange, resultLength, dropForm and more (core/native.tcl:699-705 metadata, registrations across core/*.tcl). A Botlish front end would need this exported as data or would have to query Tcl for it.

The golden 'compile' backend runs a different HIR from the front end's: an HIR rebuilt from Core IR with -strict 0. For -origin ir it skips mutvec elaboration (hir/hir.tcl:452-460), and it re-resolves struct heads against the registries. Only compile-hir, which runs only on request (tests/golden/run.tcl:202), runs the front end's HIR on the Tcl compiler.

Cache keys also need the environment. Lowering options come from BOTLISH_NATIVE_* variables (native/lower.tcl:1260-1280 and 1381-1395). The warnings policy comes from BOTLISH_WARNINGS (hir/warnings.tcl:103-108). surface::readProgramFile loads Tcl libraries named in '# requires:' comments into the process (surface/surface.tcl:52-56, core/core.tcl:36-52); that is process state outside the HIR, used by audit/direct-hir-native-path/probes/module-web.bot and by .ir/.hir fixtures.

DIRECT-HIR-NATIVE-PATH.md:204-215 ('HIR side-table ownership: carried by the HIR dict itself') does not mention the registries. Its prepareHir description (about lines 186-190) is stale against native/prepare.tcl:19-26. The design doc understates the coupling the experiments show.

verdicts.claim: Pipeline of surface::readProgramFile: requires-libraries, surface::parse, BuildProgram (NewState, CollectAndLoad -> CheckImports -> LoadNamespace recursively -> ParseModule/checks/SplitTypeDecls/LowerStatements/RemapFile into a section; CheckRef with static-site deferral), hir::buildSyntax, surface::lower::Finish.
verdicts.evidence: Read surface/surface.tcl:52-57, surface/modules.tcl:1097-1128 (BuildProgram, compileProgramFile), 477-566 (LoadNamespace), 747-788 (CollectAndLoad; LoadNamespace is reached through CheckImports at modules.tcl:679/700), surface/lower.tcl:275-285 (Finish). Matches.

verdicts.claim: The cut at hir::buildSyntax takes only plain data (syntax-node dicts + an options dict); no AST passes beyond it.
verdicts.evidence: modules.tcl:1105-1110 passes only lowered syntax, origins, files, sections, import envs and decl dicts. grep finds no call from hir/ back into surface:: (only comments), so the dependency is one-way. Two qualifications. First, the Tcl syntax constructors call core::ir::checkShape and hir::resolve::RootNames (hir/syntax.tcl:141-158), so building syntax in Tcl still needs core/ and hir/. Second, the node kinds are fully documented at hir/syntax.tcl:11-135.

verdicts.claim: Static decisions work on syntax nodes, not source text, so a Botlish parser/lowerer emitting syntax (with the static node's body and deferred list) does not interact with the decision loop.
verdicts.evidence: Round expands the syntax and calls hir::BuildFull (hir/static.tcl:1312-1338); Expand is at 445-455. Qualification: a site's key is its origin's file:start (static.tcl:406-409), and Reified writes the origin's line/column into CompilerError (static.tcl:593-625). A reimplemented loader/lowerer must therefore produce identical FileIds (load order), character offsets, line/column values and the loader's deferred diagnostics (modules.tcl:762-786, lower.tcl:803-818).

verdicts.claim: BuildOnce is the repeated unit: it resets/refills process-global registries, then runs resolve, hygiene and check. It is called per static round, per method trial and again by monomorphize. check may run CheckOnce twice, and signatures::infer and types::infer loop internally.
verdicts.evidence: hir/hir.tcl:472-541 (imports/errordecls/structs/enums/traits/sourcetypes apply, then resolve, hygiene at 529, check), 424-465 (BuildFull), 627-806 (trial/final BuildOnce), hir/traits.tcl:2250-2268, hir.tcl:878-892 (second CheckOnce with demote), signatures.tcl:248 (round loop), types.tcl:1894 (semantic rounds).

verdicts.claim: Per-build state passes through namespace variables (trait plan/cloneBindings, semantic run state, affine and completions state, staticDeferred), so builds and passes communicate through process-global state and individual passes cannot simply be moved across a language boundary.
verdicts.evidence: Real hidden channels exist. hir/resolve.tcl:1568 and hir/contexts.tcl:139 read hir::traits::Planning, which monomorphize sets (traits.tcl:2251-2267), and surface::lower::staticDeferred is set around lowering (modules.tcl:953-961). But the affine variables (affine.tcl:105-127) and the completions cache (completions.tcl:175-203, reset per pass) are private per-run state of one pass, not channels between passes. The coupling that actually blocks moving one pass is the HIR dict plus the name-keyed process registries (hir::structs/enums/traits/errordecls/imports, core::type, core::native).

verdicts.claim: Backends depend on registries the front end left in the process, so a HIR value is not self-contained. In a fresh process interp runs, compile fails NOT-A-CONTEXT and cranelift fails 'unknown type linux::path::LinuxPath'. An intervening compile makes cranelift fail with CONTEXT-NATIVE-LOWERING-UNSUPPORTED.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced with a dumped traits-path HIR (1,378,194 chars) loaded in fresh processes: interp '2 passed, 0 failed'; compile 'CORE SEMANTIC NOT-A-CONTEXT' (1 build); compile-hir and cranelift fail with 'core::type: unknown type "linux::path::LinuxPath"'. In-process, after compiling examples/surface/01-arithmetic.bot, cranelift fails with CONTEXT-NATIVE-LOWERING-UNSUPPORTED (test::Suite). Two additions. compile survives only on a core::compiler::cache hit (compiler/compiler.tcl:152-163): run uncached, or with the cache cleared, it fails with 'key "compiler::SourceLocation" not known'. Also, hir::format of the reloaded dict fails in a fresh process with the same unknown-type error.

verdicts.claim: HIR text is not a complete interchange format: -origins 1 fails on source origins, module programs fail (undeclared module bindings), and single-file programs drop methodCalls, methodChoices, flagAllowed, coroutines, semantic, contexts, affine, mutvec, methodDecided.
verdicts.evidence: Reproduced. traits-path -origins 1 gives 'origin file f4 does not match its position (ir 0)', and even import-free 15-enums.bot fails the same way with f1: the reader accepts only {ir PATH} origins (hir/read.tcl:793-795). Without origins, traits-path fails with 'binding b1 (linux::path::nul_free?) is not declared'. 15-enums.bot and bench/sum-refined.bot round-trip (identical re-formatted text) and lose exactly the nine listed keys.

verdicts.claim: (experiment) After a HIR text round trip the NIR text differs substantially (163940 vs 37477 chars).
verdicts.evidence: With bench/sum-refined.bot, native::nir of the original HIR and of the re-parsed HIR are byte-identical (828 chars, cmp equal). With examples/surface/15-enums.bot both are 1061 chars. Both programs give the same values on interp and native. Whatever produced the 163940/37477 pair was not this program's NIR text.

verdicts.claim: The Tcl 'compile' backend, as the golden runner and the Tcl test harness use it, rebuilds HIR from Core IR with hir::build (full analysis); compile-hir, interp and native do not.
verdicts.evidence: Golden runner part confirmed: tests/golden/run.tcl:84-104 sends compile through core::evalProgram [hir::lower], and compiler.tcl:582-589 calls hir::build. My counts in fresh processes: compile 1 BuildOnce, interp/compile-hir/cranelift 0. Three qualifications. (a) The Tcl harness's cranelift backend also runs hir::build -strict 0 on hand-written Core IR (tests/helpers.tcl:38-43). (b) native::prepareHir re-runs the whole hir::check for a -strict 0 HIR with violatedDeclared (native/prepare.tcl:31-58), though never on the golden runner's strict HIR. (c) main.tcl's -backend compile is the compile-hir path (main.tcl:18-19, 47-50), so the extra build is the harness's choice.

verdicts.claim: Native lowering (Tcl) reuses front-end analysis code on HIR (specialize -> types::inferRegion, range, escape, aot, ...), so hir/types.tcl cannot leave Tcl unless the native lowering analyses go with it.
verdicts.evidence: native/lower.tcl:1410-1428 (hir::specialize::analyze, range::analyze, escape::analyze, stringregion::analyze), hir/specialize.tcl:814 and 1519 call hir::types::inferRegion (types.tcl:1941-1951). grep counts include hir::aot::analyzeRegion 14 and hir::range::of 15. Also prepare.tcl:53 calls hir::check.

verdicts.claim: Lexer and parser are pure apart from core::value::isValidScalar; their namespace state is constant tables; the AST is plain dicts with character-offset spans; the parser threads state through upvar (82 uses).
verdicts.evidence: surface/lexer.tcl:477 is the only non-comment core::/hir:: call in lexer.tcl, parser.tcl or ast.tcl. Namespace variables are keyword/operator tables (lexer.tcl:66-77). 'upvar 1' count = 82. Note that errors are Tcl exceptions with errorcodes (throw {SURFACE SYNTAX diag}, ast.tcl:263-276), and node ids are structural path strings (ast.tcl:282-300) that end up in origins.

verdicts.claim: Lowering and the loader depend on the native registry and static tables (isQualifiedNative, qualifiedMembers, RootNames, coroutine native names, isBuiltinName, hir::types::constructors, $::core::libraryDir); the registry metadata is plain data (92 natives, only impl is a Tcl command).
verdicts.evidence: lower.tcl:527-529 (core::coroutines::createNative/startNative), 595-606; modules.tcl:586, 598, 613-615, 815, 862 (the cited 111-147 is the parse cache; ModulePath 149-157 uses $::core::libraryDir); resolve.tcl:170-172. Experiment: 92 natives, the same 20 metadata keys. Values like resultShape {element 0 1} and bounds {slices ...} are plain data, but they are small DSLs whose interpreters live in hir/ (e.g. types.tcl ShapeResult).

verdicts.claim: Program-observable outcomes depend on implementation details (messages with block(eN)/function eN/NAME#N, golden tests comparing message text), so a reimplementation must reproduce diagnostic order, id allocation, dict/lsort order and wording.
verdicts.evidence: Messages are observable: Reified copies the raw message (static.tcl:593-614), and InternalIds/PredictionOf know block(eN)/function eN (1046-1061). STATIC-DECISION-ECONOMICS.md:255-260 notes mutable-array messages that name block(eN). The golden suites make 125 exact rejects_message and 243 rejects_containing calls. But grep finds no golden test whose expected text contains block(e, function eN or a NAME#N rename. TYPE messages were changed to print source names (LARGE-SCALE-GOLDEN-MIGRATION.md:383, hir/semantic.tcl:859), and hygiene says diagnostics keep the source spelling (hygiene.tcl:19). Wording, including type rendering, must match; matching id allocation is needed only for bit-exact message equivalence.

verdicts.claim: The semantic-instance budget depends on Tcl's call depth ([info level] > levelLimit 700).
verdicts.evidence: hir/semantic.tcl:160 (levelLimit 700), 351 (nesting decline when [info level] > $levelLimit). Runners also raise interp recursionlimit to 100000 (tests/golden/run.tcl:59).

verdicts.claim: Time is in the per-build analysis (~76-83% of the front end); parsing 9-16%, mostly lib/test.bot (~0.19 s) in each fresh process, lexing 60-75% of parse; lowering and loading 3-6%.
verdicts.evidence: My profile of traits-path (1.72 s, 2 builds): lex 0.194 + parse 0.094 = 16.7% (lexer 67%); load + collect + lower-seq + buildProgram 0.089 s (5%); the remaining ~78% is build/analysis. errors.bot (4.23 s, 3 builds): lex + parse 9.1%. lib/test.bot alone: lex 0.13-0.18 s, parse incl. lex 0.17-0.19 s. Qualification: tests/golden/run.tcl runs all suites in one process (run.tcl:202-222), and ParseModule caches by {path text} (modules.tcl:120-143), so there test.bot is parsed once per runner; the per-suite cost applies to fresh processes (bench/golden-suites.tcl).

verdicts.claim: Within a build, hir::types::infer (with semantic walks) is the largest pass (12-32%), followed by completions/errorsets, hygiene, affine, mutvec::Elaborate, resolve, semantic::verify.
verdicts.evidence: traits-path: types-infer 10.1% self + semantic::Walk 3.5%, errorsets 9.3%, affine 8.9%, mutvec::Elaborate 8.1% (1 call), resolve 4.8%, hygiene 4.5%. errors.bot: types-infer 11.5% + Walk 8.5% = 20%, errorsets 11.3%, mutvec::Elaborate 10.1%, hygiene 6.9%, affine 6.1%, semantic::verify 5.8%. The ranking after types::infer varies by suite, and on traits-path the lexer alone (11.3%) matches types::infer's self time.

verdicts.claim: Hygiene exists only for name-based consumers (Core IR, Tcl compiler, HIR text); the native path does not need it. It still runs in every BuildOnce, including discarded trials.
verdicts.evidence: It runs in every BuildOnce (hir.tcl:529), confirmed. But hygiene.tcl:52-57 says the qualifyModules renames are HIR-level identity, not only Core IR's: hir::containers, module native targets and diagnostics key on 'namespace::name'. Only the NAME#N renames are irrelevant to native (tests/direct-hir-native.test). Hygiene also runs before hir::check, so every analysis sees renamed bindings.

verdicts.claim: Build count multiplies cost: small suites take 2-3 builds; the economics report lists mutable-vector.bot at 30, mutable-array.bot at 21, structs-and-enums.bot at 19.
verdicts.evidence: My runs: traits-path 2 builds, errors.bot 3. STATIC-DECISION-ECONOMICS.md:245-263 gives 30/21/19. Missed: most of those builds are method-call trials (21 of mutable-vector's 30, 14 of mutable-array's 21), and corpus-wide 81 of 329 builds are trials (LARGE-SCALE-GOLDEN-MIGRATION.md:400-404).

verdicts.claim: Tcl can stay the orchestrator: native::Outcome reads the run's value as host runtime values; input via argv() on all backends and read(2) on stdin under Linux native; there is no openat.
verdicts.evidence: native::Outcome/Driver: native/native.tcl:149-215 (NIR in via a temp file, value back on stdout); argv on all backends: ARGV.md. stdin read is linux::read -> linux::abi::syscall, which the Tcl backends refuse (core/linuxabi.tcl:69-71, lib/linux.bot:47), so it is native/AOT only. There is no openat function (lib/linux/io.bot:57), but the raw syscall transport plus abi::x86_64::from_bytes (lib/linux.bot:57-65) looks enough to write one as ordinary Botlish (inference, untested). Each native run is a fresh botlish-native process with its own Cranelift compile, so a Botlish front end would pay JIT per invocation unless AOT-built (native::executable takes closed programs only, native.tcl:254-280).

verdicts.claim: Language prerequisites: enums are payload-free and there is no map type; HIR ids are dense per-kind counters (vectors possible) but name-keyed registries need maps.
verdicts.evidence: The facts check out, though the cited evidence is wrong: modules.tcl:360 is RemapFile. The payload rejection is at surface/parser.tcl:664-670 and modules.tcl:829 (ENUMS.md:3). There is no match/switch either (ENUMS.md:771). The only keyed collection is ImmutableSet (from_list/contains, core/immutableset.tcl:14-23). Ids come from per-kind counters (hir.tcl:263-272). That these are prerequisites is the investigator's inference.

verdicts.claim: Module ASTs are cached only in-process, keyed by file text; lowered sections are not reusable across programs because FileIds are assigned in load order and remapped; a cross-process AST cache would be a cheap form of compile-once for libraries.
verdicts.evidence: The cache (modules.tcl:120-143, cleared past 64), the load-order FileId (LoadNamespace, about modules.tcl:519-521) and RemapFile (modules.tcl:340ff) are confirmed. But an AST cache saves only parsing (about 9-17% cold). Library code is resolved and analyzed inside every whole-program build: there is no separate compilation (modules.tcl:108-112), and library facts depend on the whole program (the erased-callable contract, LARGE-SCALE-GOLDEN-MIGRATION.md:226-231; semantic instances). lib/test.bot is 1393 of 1679 HIR expressions in traits-path (83%) and 1393 of 2731 in errors.bot (51%), re-analyzed in every build.

verdicts.claim: (summary) Compile-once only works inside one process today, and only until another compilation runs.
verdicts.evidence: True of the HIR dict alone. But the registries are already serializable: hir::format prints the type/enum/struct/refined/trait/error declaration header (hir/format.tcl:80-98), and hir::read::TypeDecls + ErrorDecls re-register it (read.tcl:76-130, 352-358). In my test, the header lines saved next to the dumped HIR dict and replayed in a fresh process made traits-path pass on cranelift, compile-hir and compile, and harness.bot ('13 passed, 0 failed') on cranelift, compile, compile-hir and interp. Cross-process compile-once is close, though it uses internal procs and was checked on two suites only.

missed: Cross-process compile-once nearly works with existing code: save the declaration header lines of hir::format (hir/format.tcl:80-98) next to the HIR dict, replay them with hir::read::TypeDecls/ErrorDecls (hir/read.tcl:76-130, 352-358) in a fresh process, and traits-path.bot and harness.bot then pass on cranelift, compile-hir and compile (experiment). The open question about restoring registries is answered for these suites.

lib/test.bot dominates every build: 1393 of 1679 HIR expressions in traits-path (83%) and 1393 of 2731 in errors.bot (51%). Modules have no separate compilation (surface/modules.tcl:108-112), and library facts depend on the whole program (erased-callable contract, LARGE-SCALE-GOLDEN-MIGRATION.md:226-231), so the framework is re-resolved and re-analyzed in every static round and method trial. Analysis results cannot be cached per library.

Builds come mostly from method-call trials in the expensive suites: mutable-vector 21 of 30, mutable-array 14 of 21 (STATIC-DECISION-ECONOMICS.md:249-260). Corpus-wide, 81 of 329 builds are trials, and the batched front end takes 1,347 s for 88 suites, against 35,857 s sequentially (LARGE-SCALE-GOLDEN-MIGRATION.md:400-412). DecideMethodCalls (hir/hir.tcl:627-806) is a major separable cost driver beside the static rounds.

The front end's type system and value representation are shared with the Tcl runtime, not only through registries. HIR analyses call core::type's algebra (subtype, narrow, normalize, integerFacts, evidenceOf, refinementOf; core/type.tcl), and HIR constants are core/value.tcl runtime values compared with core::value::equal/intOf (hir/exactvalue.tcl:192, 389, 485, 718; hir/range.tcl:767, 887). A Botlish front end must reimplement core/type.tcl's semantics too.

hir/ never calls back into surface/ (grep finds only comments, e.g. hir/static.tcl:56, 1426), so surface -> hir is a clean one-way dependency. The surface lowering is small (surface/lower.tcl 824 lines, parser 3070, lexer 485, modules 1128) against about 49K lines in hir/.

native::prepareHir re-runs the full hir::check when a -strict 0 HIR has violatedDeclared (native/prepare.tcl:31-58), and the Tcl test harness's cranelift backend hir::builds hand-written Core IR (tests/helpers.tcl:38-43). The native backend can therefore need the whole analysis suite, not only the shared lowering analyses.

The 'compile' backend survives an intervening compilation only through core::compiler::cache (compiler/compiler.tcl:152-163). Without a cache hit it fails with 'key "compiler::SourceLocation" not known' (experiment). Even hir::format of a reloaded HIR dict fails in a fresh process (unknown type linux::path::LinuxPath), so a reloaded dict cannot even be re-serialized without the registries.

tests/golden/run.tcl compiles and runs suites in one process, ordered compile -> all backends -> next suite (run.tcl:164-222). That ordering is what keeps the registries valid, and with the ParseModule cache it means lib/test.bot is parsed once per runner, not once per suite.

Static-site keys are origin file:start (hir/static.tcl:406-409), and rejected sites reify line/column into compiler::SourceLocation (static.tcl:617-625). A Botlish loader/lowerer must reproduce FileId assignment in load order and character offsets, not only node shapes, for decisions and observable locations to match.
Warnings (open question): hir::warnings::run took 0.08 s on traits-path against a 1.64 s front end (about 5%), once per program; it is a small separable leaf.

Running a Botlish front end from Tcl: each native run is a separate botlish-native process, with NIR in via a temp file and argv via --argv-file (native/native.tcl:149-185), JIT-compiled per run. Standalone AOT exists only for closed programs (native/native.tcl:254-280). stdin/file input relies on linux::abi::syscall, which the Tcl backends refuse (core/linuxabi.tcl:69-71). So a front end that reads input would be native-only, while argv-supplied input works on all backends.

verdicts.claim: Tcl talks to a native Botlish program only at process level: each native::evalHir starts botlish-native, NIR goes in as a temp file, and the value or error comes back on stdout. Program mode only.
verdicts.evidence: Read native/native.tcl:29-33 and 151-186 (Driver: file tempfile, --argv-file, open |binary ... 2>@1) and 243-248 (evalHir = Outcome [Driver run [nir ...]]); main.rs:39-49 protocol. Two notes. main.rs also accepts NIR on stdin ('FILE may be -', main.rs:39, read() at main.rs:92-99). The summary's broader line, 'Today Tcl never calls Botlish code in-process', is wrong: the interp and compile backends run Botlish in-process and return core values directly (tests/golden/run.tcl:86-101). See missed facts.

verdicts.claim: native::evalHir repeats the Tcl HIR-to-NIR lowering on every call and nothing caches NIR. For small programs the Tcl lowering dominates.
verdicts.evidence: native.tcl:126-148 and 243-248 have no cache. Measured on traits-path: native::nir took 551 ms, then 462 ms; Cranelift compile was 32 ms (`bench 1` timing line); the whole `botlish-native run` on the saved NIR took 37-44 ms; `check` took 8 ms. The two lowerings gave byte-identical NIR, so caching NIR text (or calling Driver on saved NIR) is trivially valid. That makes this a missing convenience, not a coupling.

verdicts.claim: argv is the one working input channel for text. The JIT hex --argv-file has no size limit; the Tcl layer refuses NUL; invalid UTF-8 becomes InvalidArgumentEncoding.
verdicts.evidence: Verified: a 1,000,000-character argument mixing ASCII, é, 𝄞, braces, quotes and newlines round-tripped exactly through evalHir in 209 ms. A NUL argument raised CORE PROCESS ARGV (core/process.tcl:55-63). Qualification: argv is not the only channel. Natively, stdin bytes can be read today with one read(2) per byte and decoded by Bytes equality: a test program given 'hixh' on stdin returned "hi?h". See the stdin claim.

verdicts.claim: AOT executables read the real Linux argv: 131071 bytes per argument, ARG_MAX 2 MB.
verdicts.evidence: Built an AOT echo executable (native::executable, 528 ms). A 131071-byte argument ran; 131072 bytes gave OSError errno 7 (E2BIG). getconf ARG_MAX = 2097152. Code: native/src/runtime/aot.rs:1-15.

verdicts.claim: stdin and files cannot carry text into a Botlish program: abi::bytes has no indexing or decoding, no native turns bytes into a String, no openat wrapper.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed: the API has no byte accessor (lib/abi/bytes.bot:88-90; the registry dump has only byte_store::from_list/byte_count and mutable_byte_store::*) and no decode native. Refuted in practice: Bytes support == (bytes.bot:16-17). A native program reading fd 0 one byte at a time (linux::read with a 1-byte MutableBytes) and comparing freeze(r.data) with abi::bytes::from_list(str::encode_utf8("h")) decoded piped input 'hixh' to "hi?h". A 256-entry table would decode any byte. The remaining limits are real: one syscall per byte, native only, and non-ASCII scalars cannot be turned back into Strings (no character-to-String operation), so source would live as List/MutableArray of Ints. A file could be opened with raw openat (231/257-style numbers are unrestricted, hir/syscall.tcl:30).

verdicts.claim: Each nesting level of the JIT result protocol re-escapes the level below, so strings with spaces or newlines grow exponentially with depth: about 4 characters per space at top level, 16 inside a List[String].
verdicts.evidence: Measured. A top-level String of 1000 'a ' pairs plus one newline (2002 characters) gave a 5015-character line, 4 per space; with 1000 newlines a newline cost 3. The same String inside a List gave 17033, 16 per space. Qualification: the blow-up happens only when the string needs backslash escaping (a newline or CR, a backslash, or unbalanced braces; show.rs:327-341). Otherwise brace quoting applies at every level. The same 2001 characters without a newline gave 2015 at top level and 2024 inside a List, about 1x.

verdicts.claim: In the JIT path a program's stdout and stderr land in the protocol pipe; native::Outcome ignores them, so evalHir loses io::print output.
verdicts.evidence: Ran examples/io/hello.bot. native::Driver returned {Hello, world!} {value unit}; native::evalHir returned unit. Note: native::Driver (native.tcl:151-186) does keep the lines, so a Tcl orchestrator can read them; only evalHir/Outcome (189-216) drops them.

verdicts.claim: An AOT executable prints show(result) on stdout and exits 0; a run-time error prints message and code on stderr and exits 1.
verdicts.evidence: The AOT echo printed ["a \"q\" {x}\nline2"] and exited 0. Code: aot.rs:37-50 prints 'MESSAGE (CODE)' on stderr and returns 1. The stack-overflow path writes 'error {NATIVE LIMIT STACK} ...' and _exit(1) (platform/x86_64_linux.rs:32-45).

verdicts.claim: Botlish has no exit-status facility; an unhandled declared error at top level is a compile-time error; failures must be returned as data.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed: an unhandled declared error is a compile error. A top-level call that may raise abi::x86_64::Register64AboveRange was rejected ('may produce the declared error ... neither handled here'). tests/golden/run.tcl:15 states the library-level fact. Refuted for native code: a program calling linux::abi::syscall({rax: register64(231), rdi: register64(3)}) (exit_group) made `botlish-native run` exit with status 3. So an exit status is reachable through the raw syscall today, native only. native::Driver would report it as NATIVE BUG because there is no value line (native.tcl:177-181), but an AOT executable gets a real exit code.

verdicts.claim: Recursion depth is ample: 1 GiB worker stack, and stack exhaustion fails cleanly.
verdicts.evidence: Read main.rs:66-72 and aot.rs:25-30 (1<<30 default, BOTLISH_NATIVE_STACK_BYTES) and the guard-page fault handler in platform/x86_64_linux.rs:32-52, which writes the NATIVE LIMIT STACK line and exits. I did not re-run the 10^7/10^8 depth experiment.

verdicts.claim: AOT needs every used specialized instance closed. Typed code (the golden suites with lib/test.bot) is closed; untyped code is guarded and rejected.
verdicts.evidence: native.tcl:254-285. Ran hir::specialize::regions: traits-path closed 48; examples/stdlib/hashtable.bot closed 23, guarded 4, the first being ht_should_grow (UnknownCallResultKind: `counts: mutarray` is the raw kind, hashtable.bot:83-87, 129-130). I also wrote a 30-line typed str->int open-addressing table (MutableArray[str]/[int]/[bool], hash, mod). It ran on native and interp (229) and was closed 6/6. A typed table can stay AOT-ready, but without type variables it has to be duplicated per key/value type.

verdicts.claim: AOT is the sensible deployment: 2-4 ms start-up, about 0.7-0.8 s to link; needs rustc and native/target/release/libbotlish_native.rlib.
verdicts.evidence: codegen/aot.rs:138-200 (rustc --extern botlish_native=...rlib, -L deps). Measured link 528 ms. Start-up measured 6.6 ms including shell fork overhead on a loaded machine.

verdicts.claim: The coupling is the HIR handoff: backends consume the in-memory HIR dict and side tables, and native lowering calls many hir/ analyses directly. Whatever a Botlish front end emits must rebuild that dict.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed that native/lower.tcl uses 18 hir sub-namespaces (affine, aot, blockescape, completions, construction, contexts, enums, errordecls, escape, exact, mutvec, range, specialize, stringregion, structs, syscall, traversal, types), plus hir::get 76x and others. prepareHir re-runs hir::check only for a violatedDeclared HIR (prepare.tcl:32-35). Incomplete and materially wrong as a recipe: the dict alone is NOT sufficient. Writing the traits-path dict to a file and reading it in a fresh tclsh, native::evalHir failed with 'core::type: unknown type "linux::path::LinuxPath"', while interp succeeded. In one process, after compiling a second program (15-enums.bot), the first program's HIR failed on compile (key "compiler::SourceLocation" not known) and on native (the same unknown type). Only interp still worked. The backends read process-global registries outside the dict: core::type::registry, hir::structs::registry, hir::enums::registry and hir::errordecls payloads (structs.tcl:189-210, enums.tcl:81-115, errordecls.tcl:278-312), and every build resets them (hir.tcl:472-505; sourcetypes.tcl:24-72 documents 'not built for concurrent or nested compilation'). A Botlish front end's output must therefore also let Tcl repopulate those registries, as hir/read.tcl:79-135 does for HIR text.

verdicts.claim: HIR text (hir::format/hir::parse) is not a usable interchange format: it is debugging output, fails for any program importing a module, and drops 9 side tables.
verdicts.evidence: hir/format.tcl:1. Ran: 14-modules.bot failed with 'HIR text line 2: binding b1 (mathish::inc) is not declared and is not a root name'. 15-enums.bot and 03-closure.bot parsed and gave the same native value but lacked methodChoices, methodCalls, flagAllowed, coroutines, semantic, contexts, affine, mutvec and methodDecided.

verdicts.claim: For traits-path the full HIR dict is 1.38 MB as Tcl text (traitSource 690 KB, exprs 496 KB); hir::format text 125 KB.
verdicts.evidence: Measured 1,378,156 characters and 31 top-level keys; traitSource 690,432 and exprs 495,630. The hir::format size was not re-measured. Note: traitSource is read only by warnings and the context-trait summary (hir/warnings.tcl:137, hir/contexts.tcl:1124), not by any backend, so a handoff could omit about half the payload.

verdicts.claim: Front-end time for traits-path (1.89 s): parse 271 ms (about 14%), signatures 329, errorsets 202, static-decisions 191, affine 173 ...
verdicts.evidence: My run of bench/golden-suites.tcl -one traits-path -profile 1: front end 1.76 s, parse 361 ms (about 20%), signatures 283, errorsets 171, static-decisions 171, affine 132; builds 2. The numbers are noisy under the concurrent benchmark. Missed qualification: almost all of the parse time is library modules (lib/test.bot and others). Cold, 6 parse calls covered 1186 lines in 272 ms. surface::modules::ParseModule caches library ASTs per process (surface/modules.tcl:130-143), so warm recompiles of the same suite took 1552 and 1587 ms with parse at 14-16 ms (74 lines), about 1%. Per-build phases are summed over the 2 builds static decisions caused.

verdicts.claim: Native String building is linear only thanks to virtual-construction plans; barriers (List element, capture, native operation, dynamic call) fall back to eager copying.
verdicts.evidence: native/lower.tcl:1031-1089 describes plans, plan parameters and results, and lists the materialization barriers (Ref wanted tagged, non-plan call parameter, List elements, native operations, dynamic calls, captures). Confirmed from the code only; I did not re-run the timing measurements.

verdicts.claim: Strings count Unicode scalars; char_at is O(1) on ASCII but decodes from byte 0 on any non-ASCII String, so index scans are quadratic unless the loop has the traversal-plan shape.
verdicts.evidence: strobj.rs:5-10 (ascii flag) and ops.rs:1329-1340. Correction from LANGUAGE-LIBRARY-DEFICIENCIES.md item 1 (lines 47-70): the traversal plan covers only a self-tail +1 loop from literal 0 that reads through a `peek` (width-1 substring) helper. A loop that reads with str::char_at gets no cursor in any shape. So char_at scans of non-ASCII text are always quadratic; only peek-slice scans of that one shape are linear.

verdicts.claim: Missing: a map/dict type, String ordering, character-to-String, Int-to-String and String-to-Int conversion, String iteration, character classifiers, a sort routine, type variables, enum payloads and match.
verdicts.evidence: Registry dump: no map natives; `<` takes {int int}; ImmutableSet only from_list/contains, O(n) in the reference (core/immutableset.tcl:59-67) and natively (ops.rs:1736-1745). No `match` in surface/parser.tcl. 'No type variables' is at GOLDEN-TEST-FRAMEWORK.md:298. Wrong item: character classifiers exist. str::is_tcl_alpha and str::is_tcl_alnum are registered natives over one-scalar Strings (core/tclcompat.tcl:49-51, 115), and lib/ascii.bot classifies Bytes; only UnicodeChar classifiers are missing (deficiencies item 9). String ordering, Int<->String and sorting are absent as built-ins but writable in Botlish over str::char_at plus char::scalar_value, digit tables and substring.

verdicts.claim: Present: structs (recursive declarations allowed), payload-free enums, error payloads, static traits, typed MutableVector/MutableArray, closures, hash/mod.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed with a qualification. STRUCTS.md:131-134 says a struct that names itself through its fields alone has no finite value: with no optional or sum type, recursion must go through a List, MutableVector or MutableArray, or integer ids into an arena. Verified: struct Node {kind: Kind, value: int, kids: List[Node]} with an enum Kind evaluated to 42 on native and interp and was AOT-closed (2/2). Also: a binding cannot be rebound in the same scope ('duplicate binding "t"'), so a compiler threads state through new names, recursion, or MutableVector/MutableArray places.

verdicts.claim: Cheapest path: a bytes-to-String decode native plus a file-open wrapper (or stdin feeding); return one top-level String in a complete serialization; cache NIR or build the front end as an AOT executable.
verdicts.evidence: (3) is trivially valid: NIR is deterministic and Driver/`botlish-native run` accept saved NIR (37-44 ms per run against ~0.5 s of re-lowering). (1) is not strictly needed: byte-wise stdin reading works today (verified), though a decode native would make it practical. Missing from the plan: the serialization must also carry what Tcl needs to repopulate the type, struct, enum and error-payload registries (sourceTypes, errorPayloads, enums, structs), and the Tcl side needs a loader that replays them; dumping the dict alone failed in a fresh process (see the coupling claim).

missed: The HIR dict is not self-contained, which bears directly on compile-once. Backends read process-global registries outside it: core::type::registry (core/type.tcl:81-84), hir::structs registry (hir/structs.tcl:189-210), hir::enums registry (hir/enums.tcl:81-115) and hir::errordecls payloads (hir/errordecls.tcl:278-312). Every hir::BuildOnce resets and repopulates them (hir/hir.tcl:472-505). Verified: the traits-path dict in a fresh tclsh fails native with unknown type linux::path::LinuxPath. Compiling a second program in the same process breaks the first HIR on compile (key "compiler::SourceLocation" not known) and native. Only interp survives. hir/sourcetypes.tcl:24-72 documents this as accepted design ('not built for concurrent or nested compilation').

The replay mechanism exists only for HIR text: hir/read.tcl:79-135 re-registers enums, source types and structs through hir::sourcetypes::apply and hir::structs::applyEntries. A full-dict (or Botlish-emitted) handoff needs an equivalent loader.

Tcl does call Botlish in-process: the interp and compile backends run a program inside the Tcl process and return core values directly, with no protocol escaping (tests/golden/run.tcl:86-101; core::process::withArgv injects argv, core/process.tcl:65-77). So a Botlish front end can run in-process on the Tcl backends, slowly, but only if it does no I/O.

All I/O is NATIVE-ONLY. hello.bot on interp and compile fails with CORE SEMANTIC NATIVE-ONLY (abi::x86_64::from_bytes), per lib/linux.bot:43-46. A Botlish front end that reads stdin, writes stdout or exits via syscall cannot be differentially tested on the Tcl backends; an argv-in, value-out front end can run on all four.

The library AST cache (surface/modules.tcl:130-143, keyed on path plus source, up to 64 entries) makes parse about 1% of a warm recompile: 14-16 ms of 1552-1587 ms for traits-path, against 272 ms cold, almost all lib/test.bot and other modules. Rewriting the parser in Botlish targets the smallest phase; the per-build hir/ analyses (signatures, errorsets, affine, static decisions) dominate and repeat per build.

An exit status is available natively today through linux::abi::syscall with exit_group 231 (verified exit 3). hir/syscall.tcl:30 says no syscall number is known to the compiler, so openat is equally reachable for file input.

Stdin bytes are readable and decodable today, natively, one read(2) per byte compared by Bytes equality (verified 'hixh' -> "hi?h"; lib/abi/bytes.bot:16-17 says Bytes support compare and hash). Non-ASCII scalars cannot be rebuilt as Strings (LANGUAGE-LIBRARY-DEFICIENCIES.md item 3). native::Driver's child inherits the Tcl process's stdin (native.tcl:173, open |... r), so an orchestrator could open the pipe r+ to feed it.

Performance pitfalls specific to compiler-shaped code: a function reading a program-level non-Int value (a keyword table, a set) becomes generic, as do its callers, losing specialization and traversal plans (LANGUAGE-LIBRARY-DEFICIENCIES.md item 2, lines 72-96). A constant List literal is rebuilt on every call (item 6, lines 113-128). str::char_at of a short String or slice materializes it (item 5).

traitSource, half of the 1.38 MB dict, is read only by warnings and the context-trait summary (hir/warnings.tcl:137, hir/contexts.tcl:1111-1124; written at hir/traits.tcl:2284). A backend handoff need not carry it.

Protocol escaping stays about 1x at any nesting depth for strings with no newline, CR, backslash or unbalanced braces (show.rs:327-341, measured 2001 -> 2015 at top level and 2024 inside a List). Escaping newlines in the payload (or using a newline-free serialization) avoids the exponential case entirely.
The botlish-native bench and batch modes compile once and run many times in one process (main.rs:3-6, 380-420), but argv is fixed per process, so they cannot serve as a resident compile server.
